content.text:
I submitted the verdict **part-based** with confidence 0.88, after using 44 of the 60 budget.

**Design.** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L3-S2-M4. Together these cover the rules L1, L3, S1, S2, M1 and M4. I then tested three tasks picked so the two hypotheses predict different orderings. "Overlap" below is the fraction of inputs where a task gives the same response as a trained task.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap with trained tasks | Holistic predicts | Part-based predicts | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: L3-S1-M1 | 0 | 0.00 | hard | easiest | about 17 (15 runs) |
| B: L1-S1-M2 | 1 | 0.75 | easiest | middle | about 21 (15 runs) |
| C: L2-S3-M3 | 3 | 0.19 or less | hard | hardest | about 40 (8 runs) |

Before training, A and B took between 19 and 53 examples (two runs each).

**Evidence.** Task A has no overlap at all with the trained tasks, yet it was by far the cheaper of the two low-overlap tasks: about 17 against about 40 for C. Four of its runs reached criterion after a single example. A holistic learner should have found A at least as hard as C, since C overlaps the trained tasks slightly more. Task B, the one with high overlap, was not cheaper than A, which a holistic learner would also predict. The observed order A < B < C is what a part-based learner predicts.

**Caveat.** The results are very noisy, with individual runs of the same task ranging from 1 to 36 examples. The difference between A and C is large compared with that spread. The difference between A and B is small and on its own would not be conclusive.
